generatedProse.concept-context: Across disciplines, group work is common, from a shared project to a joint report, and markers watch the process closely. They know that most real work is collaborative, and that someone who cannot listen, share the load fairly, or manage disagreement will struggle in any team. The behaviours they assess, communication, listening, flexibility and accountability, are the ones working life runs on.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students planning a group project, when a teammate proposes an unusual way to tackle the task.

{{learner-a}} hears the suggestion, says 'sure, whatever works', and goes back to their own part. The idea is neither built on nor questioned. Later {{learner-a}} complains that the project felt incoherent. The teammate was heard but not listened to, because nothing was done with the contribution. This is participation without collaboration.

{{learner-b}} hears the same suggestion and asks two questions about how it would work and whether it fits the brief, then proposes folding part of it into the plan. The teammate feels heard, and the plan improves. When a later task slips because someone is unwell, {{learner-b}} takes it on rather than let the group stall. This is collaboration: listening turned into action, with accountability.

Both students were in the meeting. Only {{learner-b}} did the thing markers are actually assessing.
generatedProse.summary: In any subject, group work is assessed for its process, because most real work is collaborative. You can now explain why markers value the process, tell real listening apart from merely hearing, and name the behaviour a situation is calling for. The next lesson looks at what happens when a team falls into conflict, and how to reflect on it.

check.body: In the worked example, what did {{learner-b}} do that counts as listening rather than just hearing?

items.text: {{learner-b}} asked how the idea would work and folded part of it into the plan.
{{learner-b}} nodded along and said the idea was fine before moving on.
{{learner-b}} wrote the idea down to mention in a later reflection.
{{learner-b}} waited politely until the teammate had finished speaking.

feedback.correct: That's right. {{learner-b}} acted on the idea, which is what turns hearing into listening.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} did with the idea, not how politely it was received.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Listening meant asking about the idea and building part of it into the plan. Nodding, noting it down, or simply waiting are all closer to hearing.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
